Danish Fisheries Industry Faces Widespread Disruption Amid Workers’ Strike

A nationwide strike by Danish fisheries workers entered its third day on Tuesday, with operations at major fish processing plants, landing sites, and commercial fishing vessels remaining largely halted. The industrial action, prompted by an ongoing dispute over pay and working conditions, is having a significant impact on the country’s fisheries sector, according to industry representatives and union officials.

The walkout, which began early Sunday morning, has seen several hundred crew members, plant operatives, and dockside staff affiliated with the Danish Fisheries Workers Union (DFWU) down tools, affecting key sites in ports including Hirtshals, Esbjerg, and Skagen. The DFWU is demanding a 7.5% wage increase and improved safety measures for workers both at sea and in processing facilities.

“Our members are vital to the continued operation of Denmark’s fisheries industry, but they have seen little improvement in pay or conditions despite rising risks and cost-of-living pressures,” said DFWU chairperson Jens Mikkelsen. “We regret the disruption, but negotiations have stalled and our members feel they have no other option.”

Industry sources report that the strike has already resulted in a dramatic drop in catch landings and halted production at processing plants. At Nordhavn Seafood Processing, one of the country’s largest facilities, operations director Maria Kristensen confirmed that processing lines have been idle since Sunday. “We are unable to receive or process any new catches. Our cold storage is holding only a limited amount of stock, and our workers are standing in solidarity,” Kristensen said.

Fishing vessels operated by companies such as Blue Horizon Trawlers and Skagen Maritime have remained docked, with captains citing both solidarity and practical constraints. “With the landing sites closed and no processing capacity, there is simply nowhere for the catch to go,” said Hans Pedersen, a vessel captain based in Esbjerg.

The Danish Fisheries Association (DFA) estimates that up to 80% of regular industry activity has been suspended since the strike began. “The impact is immediate and severe for our member firms and workers. Every day of lost production puts pressure on the entire supply chain inside the fisheries sector,” DFA spokesperson Lotte Dalgaard said.

Talks between the DFWU and the Danish Fisheries Employers Council are ongoing. Both sides say they hope to reach a resolution soon, but as of Tuesday afternoon, the strike continues with wide participation across Denmark’s major fishing ports and processing plants.
